column1: # One expected field checks the primary fold only; more fields list every
# distinct fold in order, primary first.
# Punctuation look-alikes fold onto what a searcher types.
# Letters styled with Unicode "fonts" read as the letters.
# Digits of every script read as ASCII digits.
# German-style digraphs are an alternate spelling, and ü also reads i.
# Greek: letter by letter, then modern (ELOT 743), then phonetic.
# Cyrillic: primary, common (with the string's language), Slavic Latin.
# Armenian: letter by letter, then Eastern and Western as read.
# Kana: each kana on its own (iteration marks as written), then wapuro,
# then Hepburn with long vowels collapsed.

# Ideographs keep their (simplified) surface; readings are alternates:
# Japanese seed readings use wapuro and Hepburn, followed by Chinese pinyin.
# Authored ideographs can also have a second pinyin reading.
# An unknown kanji keeps its surface.
# Hangul: syllable by syllable, as pronounced, McCune-Reischauer.
# Syllabaries read by their Unicode names.
# Thai keeps its surface; readings are RTGS, then the common spelling.

column1: # Lao reads through the same parser: standard, then French-style.
# Brahmic scripts keep their surface; readings are common (the inherent
# vowel dropped where Hindi drops it), full, and ee/oo.
# Arabic keeps a normalized surface (no harakat or tatweel, one alef, one
# yeh); readings: al- with u/i, then the first-syllable a, then el-/ou/ee/ah.
# Hebrew keeps its letters without points or final forms; readings are
# soft ב כ פ with ch and ts, then hard ones with h, tz and a first a.
# Tibetan keeps its surface; readings are Wylie with syllables joined.
# The root follows legal spelling; the silent འ is an apostrophe, then omitted.
